parts.title: Learning to swim as an adult
parts.instructions: Read the text and choose the best answer for each question.
parts.passage:
For most of my life I avoided swimming pools. When I was seven, I fell into deep water on a school trip, and ever since then I had told people that I simply did not like swimming. The truth was that I was afraid. So when my friends began planning a holiday by the sea last year, I decided it was time to change.

I joined an adult beginners' class at the Ashcombe leisure centre on Wednesday evenings, while my husband stayed at home with the children. On the first night I nearly went home, because the other people in the water seemed so confident. But our teacher did not ask us to swim anywhere. Instead, we spent the first three weeks getting used to the water, blowing bubbles and floating with one hand on the side. It sounds silly, but it worked. I stopped holding my breath all the time, and my shoulders relaxed.

By the end of the second month I could swim a whole length of the pool, although I was very slow and had to rest at the end. Last week I swam two lengths without stopping, and I almost cried with happiness. I still don't like deep water, and I probably never will. However, I have booked a boat trip for the holiday, and I am going to wear a life jacket just in case. My plan is to get into the sea at least once, even if it is only up to my knees.

questions.prompt: Why did the writer decide to take lessons?
options: A doctor had told her to exercise more.
Her friends were planning a seaside holiday.
She wanted to take part in a race.
questions.explanation: She says that when her friends began planning a holiday by the sea, she decided it was time to change.

questions.prompt: How did the writer feel at the first lesson?
options: Worried that the others were better.
Excited about meeting so many new people.
Angry that the lesson was going so slowly.
questions.explanation: She nearly went home because the other people in the water seemed so confident.

questions.prompt: What did the teacher do in the first weeks?
options: She let the learners get used to the water.
She taught them to swim a length.
She asked them to jump into deep water.
questions.explanation: For three weeks they only got used to the water, blowing bubbles and floating.

questions.prompt: How does the writer feel about swimming now?
options: She now enjoys deep water much more than before.
She is proud but still uneasy in deep water.
She has decided to stop having lessons.
questions.explanation: She swam two lengths and is very happy, but says she still does not like deep water.

questions.prompt: What is she planning to do on holiday?
options: Spend most of the holiday in a hotel swimming pool.
Swim across a bay with her friends.
Try the sea carefully, wearing a life jacket.
questions.explanation: She will wear a life jacket on the boat trip and plans to get into the sea at least once, even only up to her knees.

parts.title: Walking to school in Ashcombe
parts.instructions: Choose the sentence that fits each gap. There is one extra sentence.
parts.passage:
Every morning at half past eight, the road outside Ashcombe Primary School used to be full of cars. Parents stopped in the wrong places, children ran between the vehicles, and the noise could be heard from the classrooms. [1] So the school decided to organise a walk-to-school month in October.

The idea was simple. Children who walked, cycled or scooted to school got a sticker for every day, and each class tried to collect the most stickers. [2] Some families lived too far away, so volunteers set up meeting points at the library and at the church, where groups could start their walk together with an adult.

At first, many parents doubted that it would work. [3] Then, after the first week, the school counted the cars and found that there were almost half as many as usual. The children liked arriving with their friends, and teachers said they seemed more awake in lessons.

By the end of the month, 70 per cent of the children had walked at least three times a week. [4] Several parents said they had discovered quiet streets they never knew existed, and one father even admitted that he had lost two kilos. [5] The school now plans to run the walking month every spring and autumn.
sentences: Earlier that year, the school had also won a prize for its garden.
Teachers worried that an accident was only a matter of time.
That was far more than anyone had expected.
Not every family could join in so easily, however.
The biggest change, however, was the friendly mood at the school gate.
They said the mornings were too dark and cold for small children.

gaps.explanation: Sentence B shows the danger from the cars and leads to "So the school decided to organise a walk-to-school month".
"Not every family could join in so easily, however" contrasts with the game and introduces "Some families lived too far away".
Sentence F gives the parents' doubts, and "Then, after the first week" shows how things changed.
"That was far more than anyone had expected" reacts to the figure of 70 per cent in the sentence before.
Sentence E mentions the mood at the school gate, which leads to the final sentence about repeating the month. Sentence A is about a garden prize and fits nowhere.

parts.title: A first-aid course
parts.instructions: Choose the correct word for each gap.
parts.passage: Last month I [1] a first-aid course at the Ashcombe community centre. I had never [2] anyone in a real emergency, so I was nervous at the start. The course lasted two evenings, and there were twelve of us in the group. The teacher [3] us what to do if someone cuts their hand, and we also practised how to put a person who has fainted into the recovery [4]. At the end, each of us [5] a certificate. I now keep a small first-aid kit in my bag, just in case I ever need to [6] a minor injury.

questions.prompt: Gap 1
questions.explanation: You take a course; make, play and see do not go with "a first-aid course".

questions.prompt: Gap 2
questions.explanation: "Helped anyone in a real emergency" fits the meaning; the other verbs do not.

questions.prompt: Gap 3
questions.explanation: "Taught us what to do" is correct; "explained" and "said" cannot be followed directly by "us", and "learned us" is wrong.

questions.prompt: Gap 4
questions.explanation: "The recovery position" is the fixed expression for the safe way to lay a person who has fainted.

questions.prompt: Gap 5
questions.explanation: At the end of a course you receive a certificate; you do not borrow, lend or wear it.

questions.prompt: Gap 6
questions.explanation: You treat an injury; you cure an illness, repair objects, and recover yourself.

parts.title: A note to a friend with a cold
parts.instructions: Write one word in each gap.
parts.passage:
Hi Barnaby,
I was sorry to hear [1] you have such a terrible cold. I hope you are feeling [2] today. Remember to drink plenty of water and to get as much rest as you can. I am sending you some lemons and honey [3] my mum, who says that it always works for her. If you are well enough, we could meet [4] Saturday for a short walk in the park. [5] not, we can wait until next week. By the way, my sister has made [6] much chicken soup that I will bring you a bowl on Friday evening. Get well soon!
Elisa

gaps.explanation: After "I was sorry to hear" we use "that" to introduce what the writer heard.
"Feeling better" is what you hope for someone who is ill.
The lemons and honey come "from" the writer's mum, who says it works for her.
"On Saturday" gives the day of the meeting; "this" or "next" Saturday also fits.
"If not" means "if you are not well enough" and introduces the other plan.
"So much soup that" shows the result: there is more than she can eat, so she can share a bowl.

parts.title: A talk about a free health-check day
parts.instructions: Listen to the talk and complete each note with one word.

turns.speaker: haruka
turns.text: Good morning, everyone. My name is Haruka and I am a community nurse here in Ashcombe. I would like to tell you about our free health-check day, which takes place on the second Saturday of May at the town hall. The doors open at nine and close at four. You do not need to book, but if you want a particular time, call the number on the posters. First, a nurse will measure your blood pressure and check your weight. Then you can have a short talk with a doctor, who will answer questions about sleep or food. There will also be a free eye test for anyone over forty. Please bring a list of any medicine you take. Children are welcome, and there is a play area with a helper. Finally, wear comfortable shoes, because we will finish with a short walk around the park.

parts.title: An interview with a runner who started late
parts.instructions: Listen to the interview and choose the correct answer.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Gwilym, you ran your first marathon at fifty. What made you start running so late?

turns.speaker: gwilym
turns.text: Honestly, it was a visit to the doctor. I was forty-six, I had put on a lot of weight and my blood pressure was too high. I did not want to take tablets for the rest of my life, so I asked what else I could do. She said, "Just start by walking for half an hour every day."

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: But you did not stay with walking.

turns.speaker: gwilym
turns.text: No. After a few weeks I started to jog between two lamp posts, then three. I was terrible. I remember stopping outside the bakery because I could not breathe, and a boy shouted, "Come on, grandad!" I was so embarrassed.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: What kept you going?

turns.speaker: gwilym
turns.text: A neighbour told me about the Saturday parkrun in Ashcombe Park. Nobody there cares how fast you are. People clap for the last runner as loudly as for the first. That is when I realised running could be friendly, not just painful.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Was it hard to find time to train?

turns.speaker: gwilym
turns.text: I run early in the morning, before work, at six, when the streets are empty. The first month I hated getting up. Now I cannot sleep late even at weekends.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: And the marathon itself?

turns.speaker: gwilym
turns.text: I trained for eight months with a plan from a book. The race was harder than I expected. At thirty kilometres I wanted to stop, but a woman next to me said, "Just reach the next water station." I did that again and again, and suddenly I could see the finish line.

turns.speaker: interviewer
turns.text: Any advice for people who start late?

turns.speaker: gwilym
turns.text: Two things. Buy proper shoes: my first cheap pair gave me sore knees for a month. And be patient, because nothing happens in the first weeks.
